Nvidia jumps 31% in one day — Huang is back

After one of the worst weeks in recent memory, a single announcement from Nvidia's board turned panic into euphoria in a matter of hours. The chipmaker added around $950 billion in market value in one session, the largest one-day gain on record, and pulled the S&P 500, the Nasdaq and the Dow sharply higher with it.

By Pulse of the Economy · نبض الاقتصاد
Share this story: Share on Facebook Share on X

A week that had rattled everyone

To understand what happened on Monday 23 November 2026, you first have to understand the week that came before it.

It had been a brutal week for investors. Over the course of that week, the S&P 500 fell 8.6% and the Nasdaq fell 10%. Those are the kinds of moves that make headlines on their own, and they set a nervous tone across the market: when the two most widely followed measures of American stocks fall that far in a single week, it is no longer a quiet dip. It becomes the main conversation in trading rooms, in newsrooms and among ordinary people checking their savings.

Nvidia was at the centre of that fall. On Friday 20 November, Nvidia fell 14% in a single day. For a company of Nvidia's size and importance, a one-day fall of that scale is remarkable in itself. It also told a wider story. Nvidia is not a small, little-known company whose fortunes matter only to its own shareholders. It is one of the largest companies in the world, and its shares are held, directly or indirectly, by millions of people through pension funds, retirement accounts and index funds. When Nvidia falls sharply, the effect is felt far beyond the company itself.

The mood behind the selling was fear about artificial intelligence. For months, the central question hanging over the market has been whether the huge enthusiasm around AI — and the huge sums of money being spent on it — can continue, or whether expectations have run too far ahead of reality. When a market starts asking that question in earnest, the companies most closely associated with AI are usually the first to feel it. That is what happened in the week before Monday: doubt spread, selling gathered pace, and by Friday the market was in a fearful mood.

By the end of that week, the S&P 500 was in correction territory, a phrase used to describe a market that has fallen sharply from a recent peak. It had also just suffered a seven-session losing streak — seven trading days in a row in which it had fallen. Streaks like that matter because they shape confidence. Each down day makes the next one feel more likely, and investors begin to wonder how far the fall will go and what, if anything, could stop it.

What changed on Monday morning

On Monday morning, Nvidia's board announced that co-founder Jensen Huang had been reinstated as president and CEO, effective immediately.

The announcement was simple, but its effect was immediate and dramatic. Nvidia's shares rose 31% on the day — Motley Fool reported a rise of 31.48% to a close of $165.05, Investopedia reported a rise of 31%, and Reuters also reported a rise of 31%. The agreement between the three sources on the scale of the move underlines just how extraordinary it was: a rise of that size in a single day is rare for any company, and almost unheard of for a company as large as Nvidia.

The reinstatement changed the story around the company in a single stroke. For days, the market's conversation about Nvidia had been dominated by fear — fear about AI spending, fear about valuations, fear about what comes next. The board's decision gave investors a clear, concrete reason to look at the company differently. Jensen Huang is not just any chief executive. He is the co-founder of the company, the person most closely associated with building it into what it is today, and the figure investors most closely link with its rise. Bringing him back to the top job, with immediate effect, was read by the market as a decisive move — a signal that the board was acting quickly and clearly at a moment of crisis.

Whether that reading proves right over time is a separate question, and one that cannot be answered in a single day. But on Monday, the market's verdict was unmistakable. Buyers returned in force, and the selling of the previous week was replaced, in the space of a few hours, by some of the most intense buying seen in years.

The largest one-day gain on record

The scale of Monday's move is best understood through the market value Nvidia added in a single session: around $950 billion. That is the largest one-day gain on record.

It is worth pausing on that figure. Market value is the total worth of a company as judged by the stock market — the share price multiplied by the number of shares in existence. To add around $950 billion in one day means that investors, collectively, decided in a matter of hours that the company was worth almost a trillion dollars more than they had thought it was worth on Friday. That is a sum larger than the entire market value of most companies in the world, added in a single trading session.

A move of that size does not happen in isolation. When a company as large as Nvidia rises 31% in a day, it lifts the indexes that contain it, because those indexes are built from the shares of their member companies, weighted by size. Nvidia is one of the largest weights in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, so a 31% rise in its shares alone is enough to move both indexes by a noticeable amount. On Monday, it moved them by a very large amount indeed.

The whole market followed

The S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7,237.17 on Monday. That was its largest daily percentage gain since 9 April 2025. It also snapped the seven-session losing streak that had defined the previous week, and it exited correction territory — the sharp fall from a recent peak that had been weighing on sentiment was, for the moment at least, over.

The Nasdaq Composite rose 6.51% to 24,090. In points terms, that was a rise of around 1,470 points, the second-largest one-day points gain ever recorded by the index. The Nasdaq is the index most closely associated with technology companies, and it had been hit hardest in the week before, falling 10%. Monday's rise was therefore both a recovery and a statement: the same technology shares that had led the market down were now leading it back up.

The Dow Jones rose 3.01% to 49,595, up around 1,450 points. Its rise showed that Monday's move was not confined to one sector or one company. Confidence was returning more broadly.

And Nvidia was not alone among the big risers. Micron rose 19%, Tesla rose 11.5%, and CoreWeave rose 22% on the same day. Those moves matter because they show that Monday was not only a story about one company and one announcement. Other companies associated with AI, with computing and with the technology sector more broadly also rose sharply. The fear that had gripped the market the week before had, for one day at least, been replaced by a willingness to buy the very shares that had been sold so heavily days earlier.

Taken together, the day tells a clear story about how modern markets work. A small number of very large companies now carry so much weight in the main indexes that a single announcement from one of them can move the entire market. When Nvidia rises 31%, it does not just enrich Nvidia's shareholders. It lifts the S&P 500, it lifts the Nasdaq, it lifts the pension funds and retirement accounts that track those indexes, and it changes the mood of the whole market. Monday was the most dramatic demonstration of that power in recent memory.

Why it matters

There are two reasons why Monday matters beyond the excitement of a single day's trading.

The first is what it says about concentration. The modern stock market is dominated, to an unusual degree, by a handful of very large technology companies. Their fortunes and the fortunes of the wider market have become closely tied together. That is why a single board announcement at one company could produce the largest one-day gain on record and, at the same time, the S&P 500's largest daily percentage gain since 9 April 2025. For ordinary readers, the lesson is simple: the health of the market as a whole now depends, more than it used to, on the health of a few very large companies. When they rise, the market rises with them. When they fall — as Nvidia did on Friday 20 November, falling 14% in a single day — the market falls with them too.

The second reason is what Monday says about sentiment. Markets are not only driven by numbers. They are driven by confidence, by fear, and by the stories investors tell themselves about the future. The week before Monday was dominated by a fearful story: that the AI boom had gone too far, that spending could not continue, and that the companies at the centre of it were overvalued. Monday's announcement gave investors a different story — one of decisive leadership and a return to the person who built the company. The speed with which the mood changed, from a seven-session losing streak to a record-breaking rally in a single day, shows how quickly sentiment can turn when a new story takes hold. It also shows how fragile that sentiment can be. A market that can rise this fast on a single announcement can also fall fast when the story changes again.

But the rally is already being tested

That fragility was on display the very next day. On Tuesday 24 November, Nvidia's shares slipped in early trading. The rally, in other words, was already being tested — barely a day after the largest one-day gain on record.

That should not surprise anyone who followed the week before. A 31% rise in a single day is an extraordinary event, and extraordinary moves are often followed by a period in which investors pause, reassess and ask whether the move went too far, too fast. Some will have decided that Monday's rise was justified. Others will have decided to take profits, or to wait for more information before committing further money. That disagreement is normal, and it is part of how markets work. But it is a reminder that one day, however dramatic, does not settle the questions that caused the selling in the first place.

The doubts about AI spending, about valuations and about the pace of the AI boom did not disappear on Monday. They were overwhelmed, for one day, by the excitement of the CEO announcement and the buying it unleashed. Whether they return, and in what form, will depend on what happens next — on company results, on economic data, and on whether investors continue to believe that the AI story justifies the prices being paid for the companies at its centre.

What to watch next

The next test comes soon. On Wednesday, the United States publishes its latest inflation data. Inflation data matters because it shapes expectations about interest rates, and interest rates shape how investors value companies — particularly fast-growing technology companies whose value depends heavily on future earnings. A market that has just risen this sharply will be watching Wednesday's figures closely, looking for any sign that changes the picture.

For now, though, Monday stands as a remarkable day in market history: a company that had fallen 14% in a single day on Friday came back on Monday with a 31% rise, added around $950 billion in market value in one session — the largest one-day gain on record — and carried the S&P 500, the Nasdaq and the Dow sharply higher with it. It was a day that showed, in the clearest possible terms, how much power a single company now holds over the entire market, and how quickly fear can turn into euphoria when the story changes.

What does this mean for you?

If you are not an investor, you may be wondering why a single day in the stock market should matter to you at all. The answer is that, for most people, the stock market is not an abstract thing that happens somewhere else. It is connected to everyday life through pensions, retirement savings and investment funds. Many people hold shares in Nvidia, and in the other companies that rose on Monday, without ever having bought a single share directly — because their pension fund or retirement account holds them, or because they own a fund that tracks the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq. When the S&P 500 rises 4.73% in a day, or falls 8.6% in a week, that movement is reflected, over time, in the value of those savings.

That does not mean that one day's move will change your life. A 31% rise in Nvidia's shares does not put money directly into your pocket unless you own Nvidia shares, and a single day's gain can be followed by a fall the next day — as the slip in early trading on Tuesday showed. What matters more is the bigger picture: the market's growing dependence on a handful of very large companies, and the speed with which sentiment can swing from fear to euphoria and back again.

For ordinary readers, the practical lesson of Monday is therefore a calm one. A market that can add around $950 billion to a single company's value in one day is a market capable of very large moves in both directions. The week before Monday showed the downside of that power, with the S&P 500 down 8.6%, the Nasdaq down 10% and Nvidia down 14% in a single day. Monday showed the upside. Neither day, on its own, tells you what will happen next. What both days show is that the companies at the centre of the AI story — and the market's mood about them — now matter to far more people than just the traders who buy and sell their shares every day. They matter to anyone whose savings are tied, directly or indirectly, to the performance of the stock market as a whole.

The sensible way to read a day like Monday is not as a signal to act, but as a reminder of how the modern market works: a few very large companies carry enormous weight, sentiment can change with extraordinary speed, and a single announcement can move not just one share price but the entire market. Wednesday's inflation data will be the next piece of information the market has to digest. Until then, Monday will be remembered as the day Nvidia made history — and took the whole market with it.
